description: We are Spacehopperz, a team driven by curiosity, creativity and a shared passion for space exploration. Together, we turn challenges into opportunities, ideas into innovation, and discoveries into inspiration for the next generation!
summary: Silent Explorers is an interactive, web-based storytelling experience designed to bring the forgotten history of space exploration back to life. Developed using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js and Vite, the website takes visitors on an engaging journey to discover the abandoned and inactive spacecraft, rovers, landers and scientific equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars. Specially curated for school-age space enthusiasts aged 10–17, it addresses the challenge by transforming complex space mission histories and scientific information into an accessible and immersive learning experience through interactive visuals, storytelling and digital exploration. Rather than simply presenting technical facts and mission timelines, Silent Explorers gives these forgotten machines a voice, allowing visitors to discover their purposes, missions and remarkable scientific contributions. By shifting the focus to often-overlooked space equipment, the project makes aerospace knowledge more engaging and approachable for younger audiences. Every piece of equipment represents human curiosity, innovation and discovery. Although their missions may have ended, their contributions to science should never be forgotten. Through sharing their stories, Silent Explorers aims to inspire the next generation, encourage curiosity about science and technology, and demonstrate how past missions continue to shape our understanding of the universe. Because even when their missions end, their discoveries live on.
details:
Project Name: Silent Explorers

What does it do and how does it work?

Silent Explorers is a browser-based 3D story experience that lets students fly between the Moon and Mars and hear the stories of six NASA machines still resting there. These are Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 Eagle, the Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Viking 1, Opportunity and InSight.

The user starts in an animated 3D scene with the Moon and Mars, both textured from real NASA imagery and data. Glowing markers sit at each landing site. Clicking a marker triggers a smooth camera fly-in from orbit to the surface (explore mode). A 3D model of the hardware appears, and the user can rotate and zoom it.

The story then unfolds as the user scrolls (scroll-driven experience). The 3D scene stays fixed on one side. On the other side, a column of chapters is told in the first person by the machine itself ("I am Eagle…"). Each chapter has a NASA photograph, a science-discovery callout, and a link to a nasa.gov source. As each chapter comes into view, the 3D model turns to a matching angle. Each mission ends with an optional three-question quiz.

Besides explore mode where user can click on which NASA equipment they want to explore through the markers on the planets, user can also choose to explore the whole story through full journey mode. A "Full Journey" button plays all six missions in chronological order, from 1967 to 2022. It includes automatic fly-throughs between sites, so the user gets one continuous story from the first Moon landers to the last Mars lander.

Each mission has its own ambient soundtrack that crossfades smoothly as the user moves between scenes, which lets young space enthusiasts fully immerse into the story as they read.

What benefits does it have?

  • Makes history personal. Telling each story from the machine's point of view helps young learners connect emotionally with the science. Dates, discoveries and the end of each mission become a story and not a list of facts.
  • Learning by exploring. Students orbit, zoom, rotate hardware and read at their own pace. The quiz reinforces what they learned.
  • Trustworthy for teachers and parents. Each mission cites NASA sources. Uncertain figures are worded as approximate. We avoid invented quotes, and any poetic paraphrase is labelled as one.
  • Accessible and inclusive. It meets WCAG AA colour contrast, uses large readable fonts, supports full keyboard navigation, and describes images with alt text. Narration is written at or below a 7th-grade reading level.
  • Free and easy to reach. It runs in the browser with no installation, on laptops, tablets and phones. It lowers its own rendering quality automatically to stay smooth on school hardware.

Intended impact

We want to inspire students aged 10 to 17 to see space exploration as human stories of curiosity, persistence and legacy, not only as technology. Some of these machines/equipments worked far beyond their planned lifetimes, such as Opportunity and Viking 1. Others made discoveries that shaped later missions, such as Surveyor 3 and Apollo 12. We hope students leave curious about planetary science and engineering, and that teachers can use the site as a classroom resource. It also reminds people that NASA's machines remain on the Moon and Mars after their missions end. Their missions may have ended, but their discoveries live on.

Tools, languages, & software used

  • Languages: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML, CSS
  • 3D engine: Three.js (WebGL)
  • Build tool: Vite
  • Testing: Vitest and fast-check (property-based testing)
  • Browser automation: Playwright, for screenshots
  • Fonts: Orbitron and Exo 2 (Google Fonts)
  • AI assistance: Kiro IDE (spec-driven development), ChatGPT and Claude Code. Claude Code generated the Surveyor 3 and Apollo 17 3D machine models, since no NASA models were available.

Data and media sources

  • 3D models: NASA 3D Resources (Apollo 11, Viking 1, Opportunity, InSight)
  • Images: NASA Image and Video Library
  • Textures: Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0), based on NASA data
  • Audio: CC0 tracks from OpenGameArt.org
  • Mission facts: NASA official mission pages

How is this project creative?

  • A fresh perspective. Instead of focusing on astronauts, it focuses on the abandoned machines and lets these machines tell their own stories.
  • Story and 3D combined. Scrolling controls both the text and the 3D model, so the user feels they are reading and exploring at the same time.
  • Sound as emotion. Each mission has its own soundtrack to enhance user story experience. For example, the Opportunity track fades to quiet for the dust-storm chapter.
  • One continuous journey. Full Journey Mode links six stories across 55 years into a single narrative arc.
  • Honest storytelling. We kept a first-person voice but were careful not to present it as real recorded speech.

Factors considered by the team

  • Audience. We chose plain language, large type and short chapters for ages 10–17.
  • Science accuracy. Every fact is checked against NASA sources, and each mission links to nasa.gov. Where sources differ, we used wording like "about" or "more than".
  • Accessibility. We considered colour contrast, keyboard use, screen readers, touch-target size, and mobile layouts (responsive web design).
  • Performance. Models are limited to 5 MB, and textures to 2048 px wide. The site lowers rendering quality automatically when the frame rate drops below 30 fps.
  • Licensing and attribution. Images, models, textures and audio come from NASA, public domain or Creative Commons sources and are credited in the app. We state clearly which models are not official NASA assets.
  • Scope. As a small team, the team focused on six well-documented missions and equipment and built them well, rather than covering all NASA missions and equipment.
